lines: Riley Chen
+1 (555) 010-7731 | riley.chen@example.com | example.com/in/riley-chen
EDUCATION
Northfield School of Management | MBA | Metro City, USA | Sep 2023 - Jun 2025
Lakeview University | B.A. in Economics | Lake City, USA | Sep 2014 - Jun 2018
EXPERIENCE
Harbor Payments | Associate Product Manager Intern | Metro City, USA | Jun 2024 - Aug 2024
- Redesigned merchant onboarding around a single verification step, cutting median time to first payment from 9 days to 4 across 2,300 new merchants in the pilot region.
- Lifted checkout conversion from 61% to 66% by testing a one-page flow against the three-step flow across 40,000 sessions, then shipping it to all merchants.
- Wrote the requirements and success metrics for dispute self-service, aligning engineering, risk and support; the team shipped it two weeks ahead of plan.
- Interviewed 25 merchants and analysed six months of chargeback data to size annual chargeback losses at 1.1 million dollars, the business case that set the next quarter's roadmap priority.
- Ran weekly triage with engineering and support, closing 140 onboarding tickets over the summer and cutting the open-ticket queue by half.
- Presented the onboarding results and a follow-up roadmap to the payments leadership team, who funded the rollout to two more regions.
Crestline Logistics | Operations Analyst | Lake City, USA | Jul 2018 - Aug 2023
- Rebuilt weekly carrier scorecards used by 6 regional managers to renegotiate contracts, cutting late deliveries from 11% to 7% in two quarters.
- Cut warehouse pick errors 30% at two sites by redesigning slotting rules with the floor supervisors and retraining 45 pickers on the new layout.
- Ran the quarterly S&OP review across sales, finance and operations for 12 consecutive quarters, introducing a consensus forecast that cut forecast error from 18% to 11%.
- Led the rollout of a route-planning tool to 3 depots, training 60 drivers and dispatchers and saving 1,800 driver hours a year.
PROJECTS
Campus Food Rescue App | Product Lead | Student Venture | Oct 2023 - Present
- Launched a surplus-food pickup app to 3,100 students with two dining halls, redistributing 9 tonnes of food that would have been thrown away in its first year.
- Launched pickup reminders after 60 user interviews showed students missed pickup windows; weekly active users grew from 400 to 1,150 over the following term.
- Set up a volunteer shift system with two dining halls, filling 95% of pickup slots each week and cutting staff cover shifts from 10 to 2 a week.
MBA Consulting Practicum | Team Lead | Regional Hospital Network | Jan 2024 - May 2024
- Sized a $2.4M annual saving from consolidating outpatient scheduling across 4 clinics; the client funded a pilot based on the model.
- Mapped patient intake at 4 clinics with front-desk staff and cut the recommended intake form from 5 pages to 2 without losing required fields.
- Presented the final recommendation to the hospital COO and clinic directors, who approved a 90-day scheduling pilot at two clinics.
SKILLS
Product: roadmapping, A/B testing, user interviews, requirements writing
Tools: Jira, Amplitude, Excel

items.says: Your target role is implied rather than stated.
items.because: A recruiter should understand within seconds that you are targeting product management, not general operations, consulting, or analytics.

items.says: The strongest product evidence is buried below the first glance.
items.because: Recruiters should encounter your strongest paid product evidence first and understand the supporting evidence afterward.

items.says: The skills section is too thin for product roles.
items.because: The current product list is accurate but undersells you.

items.says: Some bullets describe activity before clarifying product judgment, ownership, or business impact.
items.because: Reduce activity-oriented wording where it does not show judgment, ownership, or outcome.

items.says: A few claims need more precise scope or context to avoid sounding inflated or ambiguous.
items.because: Clarify ownership and measurement for every major metric.

items.says: Your five-year operations background is valuable, but the resume does not explicitly connect it to product management.
items.because: Connect Crestline Logistics to product through implementation, workflow analysis, stakeholder coordination, and measurable operational outcomes.

items.says: Make the LinkedIn/profile URL visibly recognizable as a professional profile rather than leaving it as a generic URL.
items.because: A recruiter should recognize it as a professional profile.

items.says: Consider adding your graduation status or location only if relevant to your search.
Do not add a full street address.
Add a short, two- or three-line summary that connects your MBA, product internship, operations background, experimentation and customer-research experience, and the types of product roles you want.
items.because: The summary should make clear that your logistics experience gives you operational and process expertise rather than indicating that product management is a completely new direction.

items.says: Clarify whether the MBA is completed, especially because the listed end date is June 2025.
items.because: The current date range may cause uncertainty about whether you are still enrolled.

items.says: If you had a concentration, product-focused coursework, leadership role, or relevant distinction, include only the most valuable one or two items.
items.because: Recruiters may want to know whether the MBA provided formal product, technology, analytics, or strategy preparation.

items.says: If the MBA is no longer recent relative to your application date, reduce the amount of visual emphasis it receives compared with professional experience.
Add academic honors only if they are meaningful and still useful at your experience level.
Do not add unrelated coursework.
Make the scope of your ownership clearer: distinguish whether you personally redesigned the flow, led the redesign, or contributed to a broader team effort.
items.because: Potential ambiguity around ownership and measurement scope.

items.says: Clarify whether the result was measured only in the pilot region and over what period.
Ensure the relationship between the verification-step change and the reduction in time to first payment is clear.
Specify your role in experiment design, analysis, decision-making, and rollout.
items.because: The main risk is that 'then shipping it to all merchants' could sound broader than your actual authority or the experiment’s coverage.

items.says: Clarify whether the 40,000 sessions were evenly distributed or otherwise sufficient for the comparison, if you can defend that in an interview.
Make sure 'all merchants' does not overstate the rollout if the change applied only to a segment, region, or eligible merchant group.
Clarify what part of the product or workflow the requirements covered.
items.because: The bullet currently emphasizes process completion more than product judgment.

items.says: Make your ownership of the requirements and success metrics explicit without implying sole ownership of the entire initiative.
Add the business or customer reason for prioritizing dispute self-service if you have room.
Explain what 'two weeks ahead of plan' means: requirements completion, product launch, or another milestone.
items.because: The early delivery metric is useful only if the reader understands what was delivered and why it mattered.

items.says: Separate or clearly distinguish the qualitative research from the quantitative analysis.
items.because: The reader needs to know exactly what the number represents.

items.says: Clarify whether the $1.1 million figure represents annualized losses, preventable losses, addressable losses, or total losses.
Explain your contribution to the business case and roadmap decision.
Use consistent currency formatting throughout the resume.
Clarify whether you personally resolved the tickets, coordinated their resolution, or managed the triage process.
items.because: It currently reads more like support operations than product management.

items.says: Explain what 'closing 140 onboarding tickets' means operationally.
If the tickets were mostly support issues rather than product issues, consider giving this bullet less prominence.
Connect the ticket work to recurring product defects, process improvements, or prioritization if that was part of your contribution.
items.because: It becomes stronger if it demonstrates how ticket patterns informed product decisions.

items.says: Clarify whether you presented independently or as part of a team.
items.because: The current wording does not fully show your role in earning that decision.

items.says: State what decision the leadership team made and what you were responsible for after the presentation.
Specify whether the rollout to two additional regions was approved, initiated, or completed.
Avoid using funding as the only indication of impact; connect the decision to adoption, revenue, risk reduction, or operational scale if available.
Put the most strategically relevant bullets first: experimentation, onboarding outcome, research/prioritization, requirements, rollout influence, then operational triage.
items.because: The section currently reads as a list of successful tasks rather than a coherent product-development story.

items.says: Make the product lifecycle visible: identify problem → research → define solution → test → ship → measure → scale.
Add the product area or platform context if it is not confidential.
Consider whether six bullets are necessary for a short internship. Keep six only if each shows a distinct product-management capability.
Explain what you changed about the scorecards: data quality, metrics, reporting process, cadence, or decision framework.
items.because: The causal chain is not fully clear.

items.says: Clarify your role in the contract-renegotiation process.
State whether the delivery improvement was directly attributable to the scorecards or resulted from the decisions they enabled.
Clarify your analytical or design contribution to the slotting-rule change.
items.because: It currently emphasizes implementation.

items.says: Explain how you evaluated the existing problem and validated the new layout.
Distinguish between training activity and the operational result.
Spell out 'S&OP' unless the target audience is certain to know it.
items.because: The acronym may be opaque to recruiters.

items.says: Clarify what you owned across the 12 review cycles.
items.because: The current wording does not fully communicate the complexity of coordinating sales, finance, and operations.

items.says: Explain how you introduced the consensus forecast and how stakeholders used it.
Verify that the measurement basis for forecast error remained consistent before and after the change.
Clarify your role in selecting, configuring, testing, or implementing the tool.
items.because: It should be framed as implementation and adoption, not merely training.

items.says: State whether the 1,800 saved hours were measured or estimated.
Include adoption or usage information if available.
Make the training component secondary to the product/process implementation itself.
Reduce the section to three bullets if space is tight, prioritizing route-planning implementation, S&OP/forecasting, and the strongest operational improvement.
items.because: This role should not overpower the product internship.

items.says: If retaining all four, order them by relevance to product management rather than chronology.
Add a short indication of the types of systems, stakeholders, or decisions you worked with.
Clarify whether the app was live, whether it was built by a technical team, and what your specific product responsibilities were.
items.because: It could more clearly show how you made product decisions.

items.says: Add evidence of product discovery, prioritization, testing, or iteration if available.
Avoid having too many bullets begin with launch-related language; the section currently gives more emphasis to launching than to the decisions behind the product.
Define whether 3,100 students were the eligible audience, registered users, or total reach.
items.because: The denominator and measurement method matter.

items.says: Clarify whether nine tonnes were measured directly or estimated.
Explain your role in achieving the adoption and impact figures.
Ensure the reader can distinguish product adoption from social impact.
Clarify the relationship between the 60 interviews, the reminder feature, and the increase in weekly active users.
items.because: It should be emphasized as a product-learning loop rather than just a feature launch.

items.says: Explain whether other changes occurred during the same term that could have influenced growth.
State whether you identified the problem, prioritized it, designed the solution, or evaluated the result.
Clarify whether this was a product feature, an operating process, or both.
items.because: It is slightly less directly relevant unless you frame it as designing a system that improved supply-side reliability.

items.says: Explain your role in designing and implementing the system.
Define the baseline behind the reduction from five staff cover shifts to two.
Clarify the number of weekly slots if available.
Label the project clearly as consulting or client work, but make your individual ownership visible.
items.because: Make your individual ownership visible.

items.says: Ensure the client name is handled consistently with confidentiality expectations.
Place this project below the product venture if your target is product management.
Clarify your specific contribution to the $2.4 million estimate.
items.because: Precision will protect your credibility.

items.says: Explain the assumptions behind the annual savings figure.
Distinguish between a modeled opportunity and realized savings.
items.because: ‘Sized’ and ‘annual saving’ can sound like realized financial impact if not carefully qualified.

items.says: State what the client funded: the pilot, the recommendation, or implementation work.
Clarify how you evaluated that required fields were not lost.
items.because: The benefit is currently implied rather than demonstrated.

items.says: State whether front-desk staff and patients participated in the process.
Connect the reduction in form length to an expected outcome such as lower completion burden, faster intake, or fewer errors if you have evidence.
Clarify your personal role in developing and presenting the recommendation.
items.because: Approval is not the same as implementation or impact.

items.says: Identify what decision the COO and directors approved.
State whether the pilot launched and, if so, include early results; otherwise keep the wording focused on approval rather than outcome.
Add the product capabilities demonstrated in your experience, not just the activities you performed.
items.because: The section does not yet signal product strategy, discovery, analytics, or delivery breadth.

items.says: Organize skills into meaningful categories such as product discovery, experimentation/analytics, product delivery, and stakeholder management.
Include prioritization, roadmap development, funnel analysis, user research, product requirements, launch management, and cross-functional collaboration only if you can defend them in an interview.
Avoid listing a skill if it appears nowhere in the experience or project sections.
Clarify your level of familiarity where appropriate.
items.because: Recruiters often scan for analytics, collaboration, prototyping, and delivery tools.

items.says: Add tools used in the bullets if they are relevant and defensible.
Consider including SQL, Tableau, Looker, Figma, Productboard, Notion, or other tools only if you actually used them.
Separate analytical tools from product-delivery tools if the list grows.
Do not include tools merely to satisfy perceived keyword expectations.
Use consistent bullet indentation and line spacing.
items.because: Formatting should help the reader find evidence quickly rather than make them work through dense text.

items.says: Keep dates aligned consistently.
Use consistent capitalization for product and tool names.
Use one currency convention throughout.
Ensure every bullet fits cleanly on the page and does not leave awkward single-word or short-line wraps.
Use bolding sparingly for employer names, roles, or major metrics—not every number.
Give professional experience more visual priority than projects.
items.because: Recruiters should encounter your strongest paid product evidence first.

items.says: Make the Harbor Payments role visually dominant.
Keep education compact.
Consider placing Skills before Projects only if the skills section is expanded enough to provide meaningful value; otherwise leave it after experience and projects.
Aim for one page if you can preserve the strongest evidence without reducing readability.
items.because: You have enough relevant experience for a strong one-page early-career product resume.

items.says: If the resume requires two pages, ensure the second page contains substantial content and does not consist primarily of a small project or skills list.
Do not remove quantified achievements simply to force a one-page format.
items.because: Content quality should take priority over an overly compressed layout.
